extracted.intended_audience: students, general readers, and scholars researching Margaret Mitchell's Gone with the Wind (literary analysis and historical/critical context)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts critical dimensions, thematic elements, historical accuracy, reception, and production/publication facts used to evaluate or contextualize the novel Gone with the Wind. Suitable for annotating or assessing the work across literary, historical, and cultural criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title origin and metaphorical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Title phrase derived from Ernest Dowson's poem 'Non Sum Qualis Eram Bonae sub Regno Cynarae' and alludes to erotic loss as well as the demise of a way of life in the antebellum South.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page links the novel's title both to Dowson's poem (erotic loss) and to Scarlett O'Hara's invocation of 'Tara'—the phrase functions as a metaphor for cultural decline; also notes a possible influence from James Joyce's Ulysses. Use these intertextual origins when interpreting thematic resonance of the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: coming-of-age / chronological arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel arranged chronologically as a Bildungsroman following Scarlett O'Hara from adolescence to adulthood (ages 16 to 28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitchell used a smooth linear narrative structure noted for 'readability'; plot is rich with vivid characters. Evaluate pacing, chronological coherence, and degree to which protagonist's moral/psychological growth is depicted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification (historical romance vs historical novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often placed in the historical romance subgenre, though some scholars (e.g., Pamela Regis) argue it is more appropriately classified as a historical novel because it lacks all the elements of the romance genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying the work, consider presence/absence of romance-genre conventions, the centrality of historical setting, and erotic/historical elements (some label it 'erotic historical').

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery functions as a backdrop; the novel is written from the perspective and values of an enslaver and tends to present slaves as docile and happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how slavery is narrated (background vs central), whether enslaved characters are individualized or stereotyped, and how the portrayal supports or challenges Lost Cause narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of caste/class system
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are organized into two basic groups: the white planter class and the black house servant class; house servants occupy the highest 'caste' among enslaved people while field workers are lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine class stratification within both white and enslaved communities, the novel's internal social hierarchy, and implications for power dynamics and characterization (e.g., who 'stays' after emancipation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of Mammy and the 'faithful, devoted slave' archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: Mammy is portrayed as duty-bound, faithful, and devoted; she never considers life away from Tara and embodies the romanticized mammy figure common in Southern literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how Mammy's portrayal reinforces sentimental/romanticized images of enslaved people; note historical antecedents (e.g., 1918 'The Old Black Mammy') and scholarly critique (e.g., Micki McElya).

rubrics_metrics.name: Southern belle archetype and heroine characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The southern belle is an archetype for the antebellum upper-class young woman; Scarlett is a classic southern belle (charming though not beautiful) who partly rebels against the code of behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Scarlett against southern belle ideals (social skills, marriage as goal) and analyze 'bad belle' traits (deceitfulness, shrewdness) versus 'good belle' traits (trust, self-sacrifice) in how they enable survival and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical background accuracy and social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of women's roles, marriage expectations, and other social conventions are presented, but some historical details (e.g., women's involvement in business during Reconstruction) conflict with typical historical norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity to historical norms (labor roles, women in business, nursing in war hospitals) and compare to documented history; the Atlanta Historical Society exhibit questioned some portrayals (e.g., Scarlett running a sawmill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of Civil War battles and campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel mentions or depicts several Civil War battles and campaigns (Seven Days Battles, Fredericksburg, Gettysburg, Chickamauga, Chattanooga, Atlanta Campaign, Sherman's March to the Sea, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the novel's use of military events for narrative effect, accuracy of descriptions, and how battle scenes shape characters and themes (e.g., loss, survival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of manhood and masculinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Male characters are used to critique southern masculinity—Ashley Wilkes is effeminate or 'pallid', others lack 'manliness'; even Rhett Butler is described as 'gay-coded'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze constructions of masculinity, gender norms, and how male characters' traits (impotence, effeminacy, dandyism) relate to post-war Southern identity and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of 'scallawags' and social types
rubrics_metrics.description: Scallawag defined as a white Southerner who accepted Republican reforms; the novel portrays various 'scoundrels'—scallawags, Yankees, carpetbaggers, Republicans, prostitutes, overseers—with Rhett accused of being a 'damned Scallawag'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social caricatures, note how labels and epithets are used to mark legitimacy/otherness and to construct moral judgments about postwar actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme: survival (gumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitchell stated the novel's central theme is survival—what qualities enable some people to endure catastrophes; she wrote about people with 'gumption.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret characters and plot arcs in light of survival as organizing theme; assess how 'gumption' manifests in choices, resilience, and moral ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitchell's use of color—especially red, green, and hues related to Scarlett—is symbolic and open to interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring color imagery and relate it to character psychology, thematic emphasis, and symbolic associations (passion, jealousy, renewal, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of Irishness and ethnic stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel treats African Americans and Irish Americans 'in precisely the same way' according to some scholars; ethnic slurs and Irish stereotypes pervade the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethnic representation, stereotyping, and hierarchy; consult scholarship (e.g., David O'Connell, Geraldine Higgins) on how Irishness is portrayed relative to race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary critical reception and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: The book was a bestseller with generally positive reviews praising readability, though some critics (e.g., NYT reviewer Ralph Thompson) criticized its length and suggested it should have been edited down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical critical responses (sales figures, magazine reviews), noting specific praises (readability, vivid characters) and criticisms (excessive length, need for greater discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly critique on race, ethnicity, and social issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel has been criticized for stereotypical and derogatory portrayals of African Americans and for promoting plantation values and white supremacy; scholars have labeled it 'profoundly racist and profoundly wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scholarly critiques to evaluate the novel's racial politics, language (use of racial slurs), and its impact on cultural memory and education; consider modern reassessments (e.g., post-George Floyd debates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of Reconstruction and historical inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics say Mitchell downplayed KKK violence and perpetuated myths about Reconstruction; some errors reflect historical ignorance common to her era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine depictions of Reconstruction-era politics and violence for accuracy, omissions (e.g., role of KKK), and alignment with Lost Cause narratives; weigh authorial knowledge against later historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, recognition, and popular rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: Won the 1937 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and National Book Award; high sales (over 30 million copies by 2010) and high placement in polls (e.g., #2 in Harris poll behind the Bible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing cultural stature, factor in awards, sales, poll rankings, and enduring popularity across demographics and geographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel has frequently been the center of controversy and has been banned or challenged (e.g., Anaheim 1978 ban; Waukegan 1984 challenge citing racism and the use of racial slurs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider contexts and reasons for censorship challenges, specific local actions, and how contested status affects teaching, library inclusion, and public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations across media
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapted into the 1939 Academy Award–winning film, multiple musicals, stage productions, a ballet, and audiobook editions (e.g., 1998 unabridged audiobook narrated by Liza Ross).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how adaptations interpret or alter themes, characterizations, and events; note medium-specific changes and public reception of major adaptations (especially the 1939 film).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between novel and film
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific scene differences highlighted: e.g., the staircase scene (in the novel Scarlett cries out; film tones it down); an intended rape scene at Shantytown differs in perpetrators' race between novel and film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing novel and film, identify altered scenes, sanitized or reinterpreted content, and implications for character agency and racial representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place in American literature and curated lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Included in the Library of Congress 'Books That Shaped America' list and frequently discussed in debates about the Great American Novel; used as a reference point in broader literary conversations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the novel's canonical status, its role in shaping cultural narratives, and its inclusion on curated lists and exhibitions (e.g., Library of Congress 'Celebration of the Book').

rubrics_metrics.name: Author estate, rights, and legal/control issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Details on Margaret Mitchell's estate: trademark and literary-rights bequest, estate-authorized sequels, and legal attempts to suppress derivative works (e.g., Suntrust v. Houghton Mifflin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider estate control and authorization as factors shaping authorized/unathorized sequels, adaptations, and legal contests over derivative works and parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication history and manuscript preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Original manuscript fragments preserved; many draft chapters survived while others were burned; last four chapters held by Pequot Library; first printings and release history (June 30, 1936).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying textual history, consult archival holdings, printing history, and known lost/destroyed materials to assess editorial history and textual variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequels, prequels, unauthorized works, and fan fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Estate-authorized sequels (e.g., Scarlett), authorized prequels and other sequel works exist; unauthorized sequels and legal disputes occurred; fan fiction proliferates online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate authorized continuations from unauthorized ones; consider legal outcomes (parody defenses) and how derivative works reshape or critique the original's perspective (e.g., The Wind Done Gone retelling enslaved people's viewpoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright status by jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Public domain status varies: public domain in Australia and Canada since 1999; entered public domain in the EU on Jan 1, 2020; U.S. copyright extended until Jan 1, 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check jurisdiction-specific copyright law when reprinting, adapting, or distributing the text; public-domain status affects availability of editions and derivative creations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legacy and influence of the 'Lost Cause' narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel contributed to persistence of a 'Lost Cause' representation of the Old South, romanticizing plantation life and influencing public memory of the Civil War and Reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the novel's ideological influence on popular understandings of Southern history, its role in reconciliationist narratives, and critique its cultural consequences (e.g., sanitizing slavery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into popular culture and parodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive presence in popular culture: parodies (Carol Burnett Show curtain dress), references in other novels (The Outsiders), MAD magazine and MADtv sketches, and many more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instances of parody and popular reference as indicators of cultural saturation; examine how parodies reframe or critique original themes and characters.
